Like the green shamrocks Irish Catholics pin to their lapels in support of St. Patrick himself, Chicago wears its Irish pride on its sleeve.

While early Irish immigrants to the United States were often met with contempt and disregard, including in Chicago (think of poor Catherine O’Leary and her scapegoat cow), today the city revels in the Emerald Isle’s heritage and descendants with celebrations across town — including the famous dyeing of the Chicago River.

But the massive parade Downtown,  isn’t the only Irish pageant on display for St. Patrick’s Day. There are three others: The South Side Irish St. Patrick’s Day Parade, Northwest Side Irish St. Patrick’s Day Parade and Chicago Working Families’ Archer Ave. St. Patrick’s Day Parade.

All four parades take place the same weekend this year: March 14-15.

Each week, their father, an Indian immigrant who settled in Chicago in the 1980s, would pull a $20 bill from his wallet and send his children outside with the money — enough for a week of snacks and Slurpees, Ahmed said. “I’ve had, like, five root canals,” Ahmed said. The 31-year-old with a sweet tooth has brought that kid-in-a-candy-shop joy to Lakeview with the launch of Johnny’s Dirty Soda and Snacks, 1722 W. Belmont Ave. Johnny’s is a nickname for one of his brothers-in-law. The store, which Ahmed opened in December with his sisters and brothers-in-law, sells the nonalcoholic, flavor- and creamer-enhanced fountain drinks popularized on TikTok. It’s the first standalone dirty soda shop in Chicago, Ahmed said. The CTA unveiled an expanded security plan last week after federal officials warned the agency it could lose a $50 million grant if it didn’t take stronger action to improve safety on the system. The proposal includes an increase in police patrol hours, the deployment of Cook County sheriff’s deputies on trains, new fare enforcement measures aimed at reducing fare evasion and additional social service outreach to transit passengers in crisis. Some commuters say a stronger law enforcement presence could help deter disruptive behavior and make riders feel safer. Ramirez has called the North Side park home for about five years. In the past two years, Ramirez said he’s experienced three encampment sweeps at Legion Park. “I’m going to a church for today, but I don’t know about next week, or after that,” Ramirez said as he fiddled with a hand warmer. Chicago Police officers, Park District employees and city outreach workers spent early Tuesday morning clearing the encampment, which had been located in the park between Peterson and Bryn Mawr avenues. A crowd of more than 30 advocates also braved below-freezing temperatures to protest the sweep. “Until there are accessible housing options for everyone experiencing homelessness across the whole city, people need public spaces in order to survive,” Mary Tarullo, director of city policy with the Chicago Coalition to End Homelessness, told Block Club Tuesday. Gabriel, a member of the group Parks for All, who declined to share his last name out of fear of retaliation, said police were already at the park when advocates arrived at 6 a.m. on Tuesday. By 7:30 a.m., police tape encircled the encampment. Paczki Day this year falls on Tuesday, Feb. 17 and as usual, bakeries in the city and suburbs are firing up their fryers and taking preorders to meet demand. Paczki, pronounced “pownch-key,” were devised as a way to use up decadent ingredients before Lent. They’re made from a rich yeasted dough that’s fried, filled with jam, custard or fruit, and covered with powdered sugar. The list of traditional flavors is long and includes apricot, custard, prune and rose. Marimar Martinez was shot multiple times by federal immigration agents during an October clash in Brighton Park. Agents alleged Martinez chased them and rammed her car into an agent’s car, claims Martinez and her attorney disputed. Martinez was charged with assaulting, impeding and interfering with a federal law enforcement officer. The U.S. Attorney’s Office dropped the charges after Martinez’s lawyer argued that body camera footage contradicted Border Patrol’s version of events. The evidence had been under seal but was ordered released after Martinez’s attorney, Chris Parente, argued that because top federal officials continued to label Martinez a “domestic terrorist,” the public should be allowed to review the facts for itself. Evidence released Wednesday includes text messages from the phone of the Border Patrol agent who shot her, Charles Exum, plus body camera footage of agents Adam J. Perkins and Lorenzo Cordero, who were also in the vehicle involved. The evidence released also includes FBI reports and emails. Body camera footage and the incident report from the shooting, which was reviewed by Block Club Chicago, contradict Exum’s account that Martinez tried to run him over and instead indicate she was attempting to drive away, actions that conflict with use-of-force training provided to agents. The footage also shows Cordero and Perkins drawing their weapons while inside the moving vehicle and pointing them towards a nearby vehicle before crashing into Martinez’s car less than one minute later.
